stem: A school wants to check that its online typing test gives consistent results. Eight students take the test, and take it again a week later. Their speeds, in words per minute, are shown.

\[\def\arraystretch{1.35}\begin{array}{|l|cccccccc|}\hline \text{Student} & A & B & C & D & E & F & G & H \\ \hline \text{First test} & 42 & 55 & 38 & 61 & 47 & 52 & 35 & 58 \\ \hline \text{Second test} & 45 & 53 & 40 & 63 & 44 & 55 & 37 & 56 \\ \hline \end{array}\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the name of this way of checking reliability.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find Pearson's product-moment correlation coefficient, \(r\), between the two sets of results.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Comment on the reliability of the test.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why a high value of \(r\) does not show that the test is a valid measure of typing skill.

idea: A test is reliable if it gives similar results when repeated under the same conditions. Giving the same test twice and correlating the results is test–retest reliability. Validity is a different question: whether the test measures what it is meant to measure.

solution.label: a
steps: The same test is given to the same people at two different times.

solution.label: b
steps: Enter both lists in the calculator: \(r = 0.9653\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: \(r\) is close to 1: students who scored high the first time also scored high the second time.
solution.answer: Strong positive correlation, so the test appears reliable

solution.label: d
steps: A test can give consistent results and still measure the wrong thing (for example, it might reward copying familiar words rather than real typing skill).
solution.answer: Reliability shows the results are consistent, not that the test measures typing skill

stem: The table shows the resale value, \(V\) dollars, of a model of smartphone \(t\) months after it is released.
\[\def\arraystretch{1.35}\begin{array}{|l|ccccccc|}\hline \text{\(t\)} & 0 & 6 & 12 & 18 & 24 & 30 & 36 \\ \hline \text{\(V\)} & 820 & 640 & 515 & 400 & 330 & 255 & 205 \\ \hline \end{array}\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the equation of the regression line of \(V\) on \(t\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: By finding the regression line of \(\ln V\) on \(t\), find a model of the form \(V = ae^{bt}\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The sum of the squared residuals for the linear model is 12 143, to the nearest whole number. Find the sum of the squared residuals for the exponential model, using the original values of \(V\), and hence state which model fits the data better.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use the better model to predict the resale value 42 months after release.

idea: Taking logarithms turns \(V = ae^{bt}\) into the straight line \(\ln V = \ln a + bt\). The sum of the squared residuals, \(\sum (V - \hat{V})^{2}\), measures how far the data are from a model; the smaller it is, the better the fit.

solution.label: a
steps: Linear regression on the calculator: gradient \(-16.66\ldots\), intercept \(752.1\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: Regression of \(\ln V\) on \(t\): \(\ln V = -0.03835\ldots t + 6.700\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: Find each predicted value \(812.7\ldots e^{-0.03835\ldots t}\), subtract it from the data value, square and add: \(\sum (V - \hat{V})^{2} = 189.4\ldots\)

stem: A biologist records the resting heart rate, \(H\) beats per minute, and the body mass, \(M\) kg, of seven mammals.

\[\def\arraystretch{1.35}\begin{array}{|ccc|}\hline \text{Animal} & M & H \\ \hline \text{mouse} & 0.025 & 640 \\ \text{rat} & 0.3 & 320 \\ \text{rabbit} & 2.5 & 190 \\ \text{dog} & 30 & 103 \\ \text{human} & 70 & 78 \\ \text{horse} & 450 & 52 \\ \text{elephant} & 3000 & 35 \\ \hline \end{array}\]
She thinks that a model of the form \(H = aM^{b}\) will fit the data.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the equation of the regression line of \(\ln H\) on \(\ln M\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find the values of \(a\) and \(b\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the coefficient of determination, \(R^{2}\), for the regression in part (a), and interpret it.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Use the model to estimate the resting heart rate of a 5 kg cat.

idea: Taking logarithms of \(H = aM^{b}\) gives \(\ln H = \ln a + b\ln M\), a straight line in \(\ln M\) and \(\ln H\). \(R^{2}\) is the proportion of the variation in \(\ln H\) that the line explains.

solution.label: a
steps: Make lists of \(\ln M\) and \(\ln H\) and use linear regression.

solution.label: c
solution.answer: \(R^{2} = 0.998\): the model explains 99.8 % of the variation in \(\ln H\), so it fits very well

stem: An agricultural trial measures the yield of wheat, \(Y\) tonnes per hectare, for different amounts of nitrogen fertiliser, \(N\) kg per hectare.
\[\def\arraystretch{1.35}\begin{array}{|l|cccccc|}\hline \text{\(N\)} & 0 & 40 & 80 & 120 & 160 & 200 \\ \hline \text{\(Y\)} & 3.1 & 4.5 & 5.2 & 5.8 & 6.0 & 5.6 \\ \hline \end{array}\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the least squares quadratic regression model \(Y = pN^{2} + qN + c\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the sum of the squared residuals for this model.

parts.label: c
parts.text: An adviser suggests the model \(Y = 3.2 + 0.035N - 0.00011N^{2}\). Find its sum of squared residuals, and explain why it could not have been smaller than your answer to part (b).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Using the unrounded coefficients of your model from part (a), find the amount of fertiliser that gives the greatest yield, and that yield.

idea: The least squares quadratic is, by definition, the quadratic with the smallest possible sum of squared residuals for these data. The vertex of \(pN^{2} + qN + c\) is at \(N = -\dfrac{q}{2p}\).

solution.label: b
steps: Square and add the six differences between the data and the model: \(0.02771\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: The residuals for the adviser's model are \(-0.1, 0.076, -0.096, -0.016, 0.016, -0.2\); their squares add to \(0.06550\ldots\)
Least squares regression chooses the coefficients that make this sum as small as possible, so no other quadratic can do better on these data.
solution.answer: 0.0655; the least squares quadratic has the smallest possible sum for any quadratic

solution.label: d
solution.answer: 151 kg per hectare, giving 5.93 tonnes per hectare

stem: A taxi charges a fixed fee of $3.50 plus $1.20 per km, so the fare for a trip of \(D\) km is \(F = 3.5 + 1.2D\) dollars. The trip length \(D\) has mean 8.4 km and standard deviation 3.1 km.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the mean fare.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the standard deviation of the fare.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the mean and the standard deviation of the total fare for two independent trips.

idea: \(\text{E}(a + bX) = a + b\,\text{E}(X)\) and \(\text{Var}(a + bX) = b^{2}\,\text{Var}(X)\): adding a constant shifts the values but does not spread them. For independent variables, variances add.

solution.label: c
steps: Variance: \(13.83\ldots + 13.83\ldots = 27.67\ldots\), so the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{27.67\ldots} = 5.260\ldots\)

stem: A furniture shop times ten customers assembling the same flat-pack chair. Their times, in minutes, are:

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find unbiased estimates of the mean and the variance of the assembly time of all customers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Assume the assembly time is normally distributed, with your estimates as its mean and variance. Find the probability that a customer takes more than 35 minutes.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The shop's advert says that most people assemble the chair in under half an hour. Use your model to comment on this claim.

idea: The sample mean \(\bar{x}\) is an unbiased estimate of \(\mu\). The unbiased estimate of the variance divides by \(n - 1\), not \(n\): \(s_{n-1}^{2} = \dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^{2}}{n - 1}\).

solution.label: c
solution.answer: About 69 % finish in under 30 minutes, so the claim is supported

stem: A sign in a lift says: ‘Maximum load 630 kg, 8 persons’. The masses of adults who use the lift are normally distributed with mean 78 kg and standard deviation 11 kg. Assume the masses of different people are independent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Eight adults enter the lift. Find the mean and the standard deviation of their total mass.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that eight adults are over the maximum load.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the greatest number of adults for which the probability of being over the maximum load is less than 0.01.

idea: The total of \(n\) independent \(\text{N}(\mu, \sigma^{2})\) variables is \(\text{N}(n\mu, n\sigma^{2})\). The standard deviation of the total is \(\sigma\sqrt{n}\), not \(n\sigma\), because the variances add.

solution.label: a
steps: Mean \(8 \times 78 = 624\); variance \(8 \times 11^{2} = 968\), so the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{968} = 31.11\ldots\)

solution.label: c
steps: For 7 adults, \(T \sim \text{N}(546, 847)\) and \(\text{P}(T > 630) = 0.001949\ldots\), which is less than 0.01.
For 8 adults the probability is 0.424 (part (b)), which is not.

stem: Amira's times for a 400 m race are normally distributed with mean 58.2 s and standard deviation 1.1 s. Beatriz's times are normally distributed with mean 59.0 s and standard deviation 0.9 s. All times are independent.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that Beatriz beats Amira in a race between them.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Amira runs three races. Find the probability that her total time is less than 175 s.

idea: ‘Beatriz beats Amira’ means \(B - A < 0\). For independent normal variables, \(B - A\) is normal with mean \(\mu_{B} - \mu_{A}\) and variance \(\sigma_{B}^{2} + \sigma_{A}^{2}\): variances add even when the variables are subtracted.

stem: At a school fair, a player pays $4 to spin a wheel once. The score \(X\) on the wheel has this distribution, and the player wins \(3X\) dollars.
\[\def\arraystretch{1.35}\begin{array}{|l|cccc|}\hline \text{\(x\)} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 5 \\ \hline \text{\(\text{P}(X = x)\)} & 0.4 & 0.3 & 0.2 & 0.1 \\ \hline \end{array}\]
The player's gain on one spin is \(G = 3X - 4\) dollars.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find \(\text{E}(X)\) and \(\text{Var}(X)\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find \(\text{E}(G)\) and the standard deviation of \(G\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: A player has two independent spins. Find the mean and the variance of the total gain, and explain why the variance is not \(\text{Var}(2G)\).

idea: \(\text{Var}(X) = \text{E}(X^{2}) - [\text{E}(X)]^{2}\). For two independent spins, \(\text{Var}(G_{1} + G_{2}) = \text{Var}(G_{1}) + \text{Var}(G_{2}) = 2\,\text{Var}(G)\), while \(\text{Var}(2G) = 4\,\text{Var}(G)\) would describe one spin with doubled stakes.

solution.label: c
steps: \(\text{Var}(2G) = 4 \times 19.44 = 77.76\) would assume both spins give the same result; independent spins partly cancel each other's variation.
solution.answer: Mean −0.80 dollars, variance 38.88 dollars²; the spins are independent, so the variances add (\(2\,\text{Var}(G)\), not \(4\,\text{Var}(G)\))

stem: The volume of juice in a carton is normally distributed with mean 1002 ml and standard deviation 4 ml. A random sample of 25 cartons is taken.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the distribution of the sample mean volume \(\bar{X}\), including its parameters.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the sample mean is less than 1000 ml.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that a single carton contains less than 1000 ml.

idea: The mean of a sample of \(n\) has the same mean \(\mu\) but standard deviation \(\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\), so sample means vary much less than single values.

stem: The range on a full charge of an e-scooter model has a known population standard deviation of 6.5 km. A random sample of 40 of these scooters has a mean range of 41.3 km.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find a 95 % confidence interval for the mean range of all scooters of this model.

parts.label: b
parts.text: The manufacturer advertises a mean range of 45 km. Comment on this claim.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find a 99 % confidence interval for the mean range, and explain why it is wider than the interval in part (a).

idea: With the population standard deviation known, the interval is \(\bar{x} \pm z\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\). A higher confidence level needs a larger \(z\), so the interval is wider.

solution.label: b
steps: 45 km lies above the whole interval.
solution.answer: 45 km is outside the interval, so the data suggest the true mean range is less than advertised

solution.label: c
solution.answer: \((38.7, 43.9)\) km; to be more confident of containing \(\mu\), the interval must cover more values

stem: A café measures the caffeine content, in mg, of eight randomly chosen espresso shots:
Assume caffeine content is normally distributed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the sample mean and the unbiased estimate of the standard deviation.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find a 95 % confidence interval for the mean caffeine content of all shots.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The menu says a shot contains 80 mg of caffeine. Comment on this statement.

idea: When \(\sigma\) is unknown and the sample is small, use the \(t\)-distribution with \(n - 1\) degrees of freedom: \(\bar{x} \pm t\dfrac{s_{n-1}}{\sqrt{n}}\).

solution.label: c
solution.answer: 80 mg is outside the interval, so the shots seem to contain less caffeine than the menu states

stem: The number of items bought by a customer at a bakery has mean 2.3 and standard deviation 1.4. The distribution is not normal.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why the total number of items bought by 60 randomly chosen customers is approximately normally distributed.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that 60 randomly chosen customers buy at least 150 items in total. (Do not use a continuity correction.)

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the least number of customers \(n\) for which the probability that their mean number of items is more than 2.5 is less than 0.05.

idea: The central limit theorem: for a large sample (\(n \ge 30\) as a guide), the sample mean and the sample total are approximately normal, whatever the shape of the original distribution. The total has mean \(n\mu\) and variance \(n\sigma^{2}\).

solution.label: a
solution.answer: By the central limit theorem, because the sample size 60 is large

stem: During a meteor shower, the number of meteors an observer sees in an hour follows a Poisson distribution with mean 4.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the observer sees exactly 3 meteors in an hour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the observer sees at least 6 meteors in an hour.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that the observer sees fewer than 5 meteors in two hours.

idea: \(\text{P}(X = k) = \dfrac{e^{-m}m^{k}}{k!}\). ‘At least 6’ is \(1 - \text{P}(X \le 5)\). Over two hours the mean doubles.

stem: At a bird-ringing station, the numbers of robins and wrens caught in an hour are independent and follow Poisson distributions with means 1.8 and 2.6.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the distribution of the total number of these birds caught in an hour.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that at least 7 of these birds are caught in an hour.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In one hour exactly 5 of these birds are caught. Find the probability that exactly 2 of them are robins.

idea: The sum of independent Poisson variables is Poisson, with the means added. A conditional probability is \(\dfrac{\text{P}(\text{both})}{\text{P}(\text{given})}\); here ‘2 robins and 5 in total’ means 2 robins and 3 wrens.

stem: The number of typing errors on a page of a draft novel follows a Poisson distribution with mean 0.6 per page, independently from page to page.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that a page has no errors.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A chapter has 20 pages. Using your unrounded answer to part (a), find the probability that at least 15 of them have no errors.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the most likely number, or numbers, of errors in a 10-page section. Explain your answer.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the probability that the 20-page chapter contains fewer than 10 errors in total.

idea: The number of error-free pages out of 20 is binomial, with \(p\) from part (a). Over 10 pages the errors follow \(\text{Po}(6)\); compare \(\text{P}(X = k)\) for neighbouring \(k\) to find the mode.

solution.label: c
steps: For \(\text{Po}(6)\): \(\text{P}(X = 5) = \dfrac{e^{-6}6^{5}}{120}\) and \(\text{P}(X = 6) = \dfrac{e^{-6}6^{6}}{720} = \dfrac{e^{-6}6^{5}}{120}\), both \(0.1606\ldots\), and all other values are less likely.
solution.answer: 5 and 6 errors are equally likely (probability 0.161 each)

stem: An ecologist counts the dandelions in 80 randomly placed square quadrats in a meadow.
\[\def\arraystretch{1.35}\begin{array}{|l|ccccccc|}\hline \text{Dandelions} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\ \hline \text{Quadrats} & 12 & 21 & 20 & 14 & 8 & 4 & 1 \\ \hline \end{array}\]

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the mean and the unbiased estimate of the variance of the number of dandelions per quadrat.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Explain why a Poisson distribution may be a suitable model.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Use a Poisson model with your mean to estimate the probability that a quadrat contains at least 4 dandelions.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Using the mean 2.0125, find the number of quadrats out of 80 the model predicts to contain no dandelions, and compare it with the data.

idea: A Poisson distribution has its mean equal to its variance, so similar values from the data support the model. Expected frequency \(= 80 \times \text{probability}\).

solution.label: b
steps: The variance is close to the mean.
solution.answer: The mean and variance are approximately equal, as in a Poisson distribution

solution.label: d
solution.answer: About 10.7 quadrats, close to the 12 observed

stem: The number of potholes reported on a road in a week follows a Poisson distribution with mean \(m\). The probability of exactly 2 reports in a week is equal to the probability of exactly 3 reports in a week.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(m = 3\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability of no reports in a fortnight.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The council can repair up to 5 potholes in a week. Find the probability that, in 10 weeks, there are at least 2 weeks with more than 5 reports.

idea: Set \(\dfrac{e^{-m}m^{2}}{2!} = \dfrac{e^{-m}m^{3}}{3!}\) and cancel. For part (c), find the probability for one week, then count weeks with a binomial distribution.

stem: A spinner is meant to land on red with probability 0.25. Leo suspects it lands on red more often. He spins it 20 times and will reject the claim if it lands on red 9 or more times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null and alternative hypotheses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe a Type I error in this context.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability of a Type I error.

parts.label: d
parts.text: In fact the spinner lands on red with probability 0.4. Find the probability of a Type II error.

idea: A Type I error rejects a true \(\text{H}_{0}\); a Type II error fails to reject a false \(\text{H}_{0}\). Both probabilities come from the binomial distribution, using the value of \(p\) that is actually true.

solution.label: b
solution.answer: Concluding the spinner favours red when its probability of red really is 0.25

stem: A bus company claims that 80 % of its buses arrive on time. A passenger group thinks the true proportion is lower. They check 25 randomly chosen buses and test the claim at the 5 % significance level.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null and alternative hypotheses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the critical region for the test.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the actual significance level of the test.

parts.label: d
parts.text: 16 of the 25 buses arrive on time. State the conclusion of the test.

idea: The critical region is the set of the most extreme values (here, the lowest counts) whose total probability under \(\text{H}_{0}\) is as large as possible without going over 5 %.

solution.label: a
steps: \(p\) is the proportion of buses on time.

solution.label: c
steps: The probability of the critical region when \(\text{H}_{0}\) is true.

solution.label: d
solution.answer: Reject \(\text{H}_{0}\): there is evidence at the 5 % level that fewer than 80 % of buses are on time

stem: An online shop receives complaints at a mean rate of 2.5 per day, following a Poisson distribution. After a new checkout page is introduced, it receives only 3 complaints in 4 days. The manager tests at the 5 % level whether the complaint rate has fallen.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null and alternative hypotheses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the \(p\)-value and state the conclusion of the test.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the critical region for a test of the same hypotheses at the 5 % level, based on the number of complaints in 4 days.

idea: Over 4 days the mean under \(\text{H}_{0}\) is \(4 \times 2.5 = 10\). The \(p\)-value is the probability of a result at least as extreme as the one observed: here \(\text{P}(X \le 3)\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(\lambda\) is the mean number of complaints per day.

solution.label: b
solution.answer: \(p = 0.0103\); reject \(\text{H}_{0}\): there is evidence the complaint rate has fallen

stem: A machine cuts metal rods. Their lengths are normally distributed with standard deviation 1.2 mm, and the machine is set to a mean length of 250 mm. A random sample of 16 rods has a mean length of 250.7 mm. A test is carried out at the 5 % level to see whether the mean length has changed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null and alternative hypotheses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the test statistic and the \(p\)-value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the conclusion of the test.

idea: With \(\sigma\) known, use a \(z\)-test: \(z = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_{0}}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\). ‘Changed’ means a two-tailed test, so the \(p\)-value counts both tails.

solution.label: a
steps: Two-tailed, because a change in either direction matters.

solution.label: c
solution.answer: Reject \(\text{H}_{0}\): there is evidence that the mean length has changed

stem: A health worker believes students sleep less than the recommended 8 hours a night. Ten randomly chosen students record their sleep, in hours:
Assume the amount of sleep is normally distributed. A test is carried out at the 1 % level.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null and alternative hypotheses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the test statistic and the \(p\)-value.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the conclusion of the test.

idea: The population standard deviation is unknown, so use a one-sample \(t\)-test with \(n - 1 = 9\) degrees of freedom: \(t = \dfrac{\bar{x} - \mu_{0}}{s_{n-1}/\sqrt{n}}\).

solution.label: c
solution.answer: Reject \(\text{H}_{0}\): there is evidence at the 1 % level that students sleep less than 8 hours on average

stem: Eight volunteers take a reaction-time test, then drink a caffeinated drink and take the test again. Their times, in milliseconds, are shown.
A researcher tests, at the 5 % level, whether the drink reduces reaction time, using the reductions \(d = \text{before} - \text{after}\). Assume the reductions are normally distributed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why a paired test is appropriate.

parts.label: b
parts.text: State the null and alternative hypotheses.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the \(p\)-value and state the conclusion of the test.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find a 95 % confidence interval for the mean reduction in reaction time.

idea: Each volunteer gives two linked measurements, so work with the differences \(d = \text{before} - \text{after}\) and run a one-sample \(t\)-test on them.

solution.label: a
steps: Each ‘after’ time belongs to the same person as a ‘before’ time, so differences between people cancel out.
solution.answer: The two times come from the same volunteer

solution.label: b
steps: \(\mu_{d}\) is the mean of before − after.

solution.label: c
solution.answer: \(p = 0.00320 < 0.05\): reject \(\text{H}_{0}\); there is evidence the drink reduces reaction time

stem: For nine students, the table shows their daily screen time, \(x\) hours, and their sleep, \(y\) hours.
A test is carried out at the 5 % level to see whether there is negative correlation between screen time and sleep in the population.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the null and alternative hypotheses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the sample correlation coefficient \(r\) and the (one-tailed) \(p\)-value for the test.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State the conclusion of the test.

idea: The hypotheses are about the population correlation coefficient \(\rho\). The calculator's linear-regression \(t\)-test gives \(r\) and the \(p\)-value together.

solution.label: c
solution.answer: Reject \(\text{H}_{0}\): there is evidence of negative correlation between screen time and sleep

stem: Ball bearings should have a mean diameter of 8.00 mm. Diameters are normally distributed with standard deviation 0.05 mm. A quality inspector measures a random sample of 20 bearings and tests, at the 1 % level, whether the mean diameter is too large.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the hypotheses and find the critical value \(c\) of the sample mean, so that \(\text{H}_{0}\) is rejected when \(\bar{x} > c\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: The sample mean is 8.021 mm. State the conclusion of the test.

parts.label: c
parts.text: In fact the mean diameter is 8.03 mm. Find the probability of a Type II error.

idea: Under \(\text{H}_{0}\), \(\bar{X} \sim \text{N}\!\left(8, \dfrac{0.05^{2}}{20}\right)\); \(c\) cuts off the top 1 %. A Type II error happens when \(\bar{x} \le c\) although the true mean is 8.03, so use \(\bar{X} \sim \text{N}\!\left(8.03, \dfrac{0.05^{2}}{20}\right)\).

solution.label: b
steps: \(8.021 < 8.026\), so it is not in the critical region.
solution.answer: Do not reject \(\text{H}_{0}\): no evidence at the 1 % level that the mean is too large

stem: Each working day, Nadia either cycles (C) or takes the bus (B) to work. If she cycles one day, the probability she cycles the next day is 0.8. If she takes the bus one day, the probability she cycles the next day is 0.35.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the transition matrix \(\boldsymbol{T}\), with columns for today's choice (C, B) and rows for tomorrow's.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Nadia cycles on Monday. Find the probability that she cycles on Wednesday.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the long-term proportion of days on which Nadia cycles.

idea: Two steps of the chain use \(\boldsymbol{T}^{2}\). In the long term the proportions \(\boldsymbol{s}\) stay the same from day to day: \(\boldsymbol{Ts} = \boldsymbol{s}\).

solution.label: c
steps: Let the proportion cycling be \(c\): \(c = 0.8c + 0.35(1 - c)\), so \(0.55c = 0.35\) and \(c = \dfrac{7}{11}\).

stem: A gym has 300 members, and each member goes to one class a week: yoga (Y), spin (S) or weights (W). The matrix \(\boldsymbol{T}\) gives the probabilities of each class next week (rows, in the order Y, S, W) for a member's class this week (columns, in the same order).
This week, 120 members do yoga, 90 do spin and 90 do weights.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the expected number of members in each class in two weeks' time.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the long-term number of members in each class.

parts.label: c
parts.text: State one assumption made by this model.

idea: Multiply the state vector by \(\boldsymbol{T}\) once for each week. The long-term state is the eigenvector of \(\boldsymbol{T}\) for eigenvalue 1, scaled so the entries add to 300 (or find a high power of \(\boldsymbol{T}\)).

solution.label: c
steps: The model uses the same probabilities every week.
solution.answer: For example: the transition probabilities stay the same each week, and no members join or leave

stem: A streaming service has a Basic plan and a Premium plan. Each month, 10 % of Basic subscribers move to Premium and 25 % of Premium subscribers move to Basic; nobody leaves. At the start there are 8000 Basic and 2000 Premium subscribers.
The transition matrix, with columns for this month's plan (Basic, Premium), is \(\boldsymbol{T} = \begin{pmatrix}0.9 & 0.25 \\ 0.1 & 0.75\end{pmatrix}\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the eigenvalues of \(\boldsymbol{T}\) and a corresponding eigenvector for each.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Hence find an expression for the number of Premium subscribers after \(n\) months.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Write down the long-term number of Premium subscribers.

idea: Write the start vector as a combination of the eigenvectors. Each month the eigenvector for \(\lambda = 1\) stays the same and the other is multiplied by its eigenvalue, so \(\boldsymbol{s}_{n} = a\boldsymbol{v}_{1} + b\lambda_{2}^{\,n}\boldsymbol{v}_{2}\).

solution.label: b
steps: \(\begin{pmatrix}8000 \\ 2000\end{pmatrix} = a\begin{pmatrix}5 \\ 2\end{pmatrix} + b\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{pmatrix}\): adding the rows, \(7a = 10\,000\), so \(a = \dfrac{10\,000}{7}\) and \(b = 2\,\dfrac{10\,000}{7} - 2000 = \dfrac{6000}{7}\).

stem: A help desk classifies each support ticket at the end of each day as Open (O), In progress (I) or Closed (C). From one day to the next: an Open ticket stays Open with probability 0.3, moves to In progress with probability 0.6 and is Closed with probability 0.1; an In progress ticket stays In progress with probability 0.5 and is Closed with probability 0.5; a Closed ticket stays Closed.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write down the transition matrix \(\boldsymbol{T}\), with columns for today's state (O, I, C).

parts.label: b
parts.text: A new ticket is Open. Find the probability that it is Closed three days later.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the least number of days after which the probability that a new Open ticket is Closed is at least 0.95.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write down the long-term state vector for a ticket, and explain it.

idea: Column O of \(\boldsymbol{T}^{n}\) gives the state after \(n\) days for a ticket that starts Open. ‘Closed’ is an absorbing state: once there, a ticket never leaves.

solution.label: a
steps: Columns O, I, C; rows O, I, C.

solution.label: d
steps: The entries for O and I shrink towards 0 as \(n\) grows.
solution.answer: \(\begin{pmatrix}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}\): every ticket is eventually closed, and closed tickets never reopen
